- When sentiment is consistently negative or neutral over recent days, model tends to overcorrect upward — reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model often overshoots and fails to adjust — apply downward drag or lagged decay to forecast.
- If official supply net is negative and bullish sentiment is low, model overestimates recovery — adjust downward by 5–10% of forecast range.
- In high-event periods (e.g., >20 events/30d), model overfits short-term volatility — smooth forecast with exponential decay or reduce volatility coefficient.
- When sentiment history shows strong bearish momentum (e.g., >2/3 negative), model often fails to recognize structural bearishness — apply bias correction toward lower end of range.
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly but true outcome shows sharp decline, model underestimates bearish shock — add downward bias proportional to event count or sentiment severity.
- In low-sentiment periods (all 0.00), model often drifts upward — force mean reversion to 10–15% below recent 5-day average.
- For high-event, high-bearish context, model tends to overestimate rebound — apply “rebound ceiling” rule: cap forecast at 10–15% below peak of prior 30d.
